Lessons from Warren Buffett
In August, former hedge fund manager
Whitney Tilson
shared seven key factors behind Buffett’s success. Here’s a look at the seven items:
He’s a genius – an investing savant: Tilson says Buffett could astound people with his knowledge and memory of the revenue and profits of companies, even decades later.

Lets the magic of long-term compounding work for him: As an investor for 85 years, Buffett was able to have compounded annual growth rates of 20%, turning dollars into millions of dollars by posting historically strong returns compounded over time.
Got on a steep learning curve and never got off it: Tilson highlights that 94% of Buffett’s wealth was accumulated over the past 36 years and came after Buffett turned 60 and could have retired.

Has always been comfortable standing apart from the investing "herd": Buffett worked in New York City two times in the 1950s, once as a graduate student at Columbia Business School and later as a securities analyst for mentor
Benjamin Graham
’s firm. Later, Buffett moved thousands of miles away from New York City back to his hometown of Omaha, Nebraska, keeping him away from the herd.
Held on to his Berkshire stock when he closed his hedge fund, Buffett Partnership: Tilson said this allowed Buffett to not have to sell to cash out panicky limited partners during times of turmoil.

Recognized the power of marrying insurance businesses with his investing acumen early in his career: Buffett was able to use the "float," or money received in premiums from insurance companies before claims were paid and invest the capital. This turned into one of the ways that Buffett was able to produce strong annual returns and differentiate himself from the pack, turning the premium money into profits instead of simply low-cost capital.

Let his winners run: Most humans end up taking profits in stocks, which is why Tilson says many index funds beat actively managed funds. Buffett was known to hold onto his positions for years or, in some cases, decades.
"In conclusion, Buffett’s career is a fountain of important lessons that I think every investor can learn from," Tilson said."
